A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuArch and retain the 2,671-question benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 26 models, skill and modality breakdowns, failure analyses, and human validation of LLM judging.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark evaluations, expands the evaluated models and judge analyses, and adds fine-tuning and simulator-based architecture-design experiments.

M1.justification: v2 introduces QuArch-based model training absent from v1: filtering memory-related questions, distilling answers and GPT-5.2 explanations, and fine-tuning Gemma and Llama for iterative simulator-guided design (Section 4.4, Appendix B.6 and D.11). This substantially extends the methodology beyond evaluating existing models; the original benchmark construction and primary judging procedure remain.

E1.justification: The original benchmark retains its question count, topic coverage, and modality totals. v2 additionally evaluates memory-hierarchy design for matrix multiplication and DRAM-controller configuration across four workloads, extending evaluation from answering questions to proposing and iteratively optimizing simulated designs.

E2.justification: The full model comparison retains the original 26 models and adds GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Qwen3-VL-32B. The headline tables replace the earlier GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 entries with newer models. Appendix B.9 also adds a Qwen3-VL-235B judge alongside Claude and Gemini.

E3.justification: Section 2.3 changes the reported skill-labeling procedure from LLM classification to expert primary and optional secondary labels, revising the evaluated skill subsets. New experiments introduce two SFT configurations, ten-turn design trials with explicit area and energy constraints, and forty-proposal DRAM searches. The original zero-shot QA grading framework remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds two downstream case studies, comparisons between fine-tuning configurations, and a reported unsuccessful unfiltered-training alternative. Appendix B.9 expands judge validation with cross-judge agreement, alternative-judge score tables, and self-judgment bias analysis. Several failure examples in Appendix C.3 and C.5 are replaced rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: The existing three answer generations and majority judging remain unchanged. The added studies report twenty independent trials per model/configuration and ten runs per model/workload, respectively. Figure 15 introduces correlation and significance reporting, with r = 0.726 and p = 0.007; these additions concern the new studies.

E6.justification: Skill-based scores change alongside revised labels: GPT-5 reasoning accuracy is 72.4% in v1 Table 4 and 72.0% in v2 Table 6, without establishing a same-partition performance decline. New results include Gemma success increasing from 30% to 70% and Llama from 55% to 95% under three-epoch SFT, plus area-efficiency, controller-design, and expanded judge findings.

T1.justification: Changes are confined to worked benchmark mathematics. Appendix C replaces earlier paging and bit-arithmetic derivations with page-entry sizing and branch-penalty examples, and C.7.2 adds a refresh-utilization derivation yielding 800,000 rows per bank. No general theoretical results or proofs about QuArch are introduced.

C1.justification: The benchmark, four-skill framework, and knowledge-versus-reasoning gap remain central claims. v2 adds a fifth contribution and an abstract claim that training on QuArch transfers to practical memory design, improving design success and achieving up to 1.99 times better area efficiency. v1 presented downstream usefulness principally as motivation.

C2.justification: v2 expands interpretations concerning downstream applicability, specialized versus unfiltered SFT, and the trade-off between design success and best discovered area. It adds conclusions about judge self-preference and clarifies the benchmark's relationship to executable agentic evaluations. Revised failure analyses also remove misleading claims about endianness and bit indexing from v1 Appendix C.3.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly documents gated access, encrypted solutions, permitted judge hosting, and private leaderboard evaluation. Appendices B.6, D.11, and D.12 add training-data selection, 676 SFT samples from 45 questions, Together AI usage, hyperparameters, teacher prompts, simulator constraints, and controller-search instructions absent from v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds educational-framework, distillation, simulation, and architecture-workflow references, including ABET/ACM, s1, ArchGym, and CacheMind. These support the expanded scope, while Section 5 largely retains the original positioning against software, hardware-implementation, and general QA benchmarks. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence remains recognizable. v2 edits prose and terminology, standardizes headings and model names, moves contributor acknowledgments and ethics/reproducibility material, reorganizes appendix subsections, and adds scope explanations. Much of the retained methodological text and prompt content remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references to a two-column conference layout, rearranges the skills-framework figure, redraws distribution plots, and adds an example montage and controller-design scatterplot. It introduces training and judge-analysis tables, converts v1's confusion-matrix figure into a table, and removes the redundant frontier-only modality table.

improvement.justification: The downstream studies substantially strengthen evidence for QuArch's practical relevance beyond QA accuracy, with controls and implementation details absent from v1. v2 also replaces failure examples that labeled answers incorrect despite matching their supplied solutions. These gains are qualified by reporting inconsistencies: Table 14a totals 916 responses despite the stated 908, and Table 15 does not support the prose's self-bias percentages. Table 9 also shows that improved success and minimum area occur under different training configurations.
